NVIDIA Posts 103% YoY Revenue Growth in 3Q FY2027, Forecasts 4Q Revenue of $130B  NVIDIA reported revenue of $115.8B for its third quarter of fiscal 2027 (ended October 25, 2026), up 20% QoQ and 103% YoY. The result exceeded market expectations of approximately $109.1B.  Data Center Revenue Grows 110% YoY, with Vera Rubin Contributing Nearly $20B in Incremental Revenue NVIDIA’s Data Center revenue reached $107.6B, up 21% QoQ and 110% YoY. Within this segment, revenue from AI cloud, industrial, and enterprise customers totaled $47.5B, surging 195% YoY and representing the fastest-growing category. Revenue from hyperscale cloud providers reached $60.1B, up 71% YoY. NVIDIA also noted that Vera Rubin contributed nearly $20B in incremental revenue compared with the previous quarter.  Gross Margin Remains High, with Trough Expected in 4Q NVIDIA’s GAAP gross margin stood at 74.8% in 3Q FY2027. The company forecasts a decline to 71–72% in 4Q. During the earnings call, CFO Colette Kress described the fourth quarter as the gross margin trough and expects margins to recover to 72–73% in FY2028.  Supply Purchase Commitments Rise to $390B NVIDIA’s supply purchase commitments increased from $279B in the previous quarter to $390B, primarily driven by multi-year memory procurement agreements.  4Q Revenue Forecast at $130B, Excluding Data Center Compute Revenue from China NVIDIA forecasts 4Q revenue of $130B, plus or minus 3%, with no contribution from data center compute revenue in China assumed in its outlook. During the earnings call, Kress also raised the company's FY2028 revenue growth outlook from approximately 70% to around 75%.  📊More semiconductor news: https://buff.ly/YckK6fp 📊More NVIDIA financial charts: https://buff.ly/3AHP9WB

[Breaking] Google Reportedly Sticks With Intel EMIB-T Despite 35% Substrate Yields as HumuFish Schedule Tightens   Uncertainty is growing over potential delays to Google’s TPU v9. Industry sources point to the HumuFish variation as a key area of concern: reported yield problems with Intel’s EMIB-T substrates have raised the possibility of a switch to TSMC’s CoWoS-L. Supply chain checks, however, indicate that HumuFish remains “100%” committed to EMIB-T.  Yield Gap Raises Production Readiness Concerns According to Common Wealth Magazine, EMIB-T’s architecture poses two major challenges for substrate suppliers. First, differences in thermal expansion between ABF substrates and embedded silicon bridges make precise alignment difficult during high-temperature processing. Second, NCF (Non-Conductive Film), applied beneath the bridges’ TSVs, can trap air bubbles during bonding, potentially weakening adhesion and further weighing on yields.  Against this backdrop, industry sources say that EMIB-T substrate yields were around 35% in 3Q26, well short of the 50% target set for year-end.  However, efforts are underway. While the reported bottleneck centers on substrate suppliers’ difficulties embedding TSV-equipped silicon bridge dies, industry sources note that Intel has adjusted its substrate electroplating process, while suppliers including Ibiden, Unimicron, and Shinko continue working to improve yields.  TPU v9 Packaging Orders Split Between TSMC and Intel According to industry sources, Google’s TPU v9 lineup is confirmed to include three variants: Broadcom-designed WhaleFish, and MediaTek-designed HumuFish and TriggerFish. WhaleFish is expected to adopt TSMC’s CoWoS-L, with mass production slated for 2H27. HumuFish, meanwhile, is set to enter mass production in 1H28, relying exclusively on Intel’s EMIB-T. TriggerFish is also planned to use EMIB-T, with production targeted for 2H28 or later.  TechNews, citing analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, further explains that TriggerFish is positioned as an upgraded TPU v9 with stronger inference capabilities, designed to address both CPU and memory bottlenecks.   HumuFish’s Potential Timeline Slip Amid recent market rumors of HumuFish’s delay, industry sources indicate that the tape-out of Google-designed Compute Die A, built on TSMC’s N2 process, has been pushed back to late October, while other dies remain on schedule. Industry sources suggest the delay is expected to push back trial production of the complete package.   Taken together, HumuFish’s 1H28 mass production target still gives the supply chain time to work through EMIB-T’s issues, but a tape-out that slips to January 2027 could compress that cushion. How quickly substrate yields climb, and whether design milestones hold, will determine if HumuFish stays on schedule. The outcome will also be a key test of Intel’s ability to win large external customers for advanced packaging.   More: https://buff.ly/8COdCZX 🔗  #Google #TPU #Intel #EMIB

[OCP in Focus] Arm Targets $300B CPU Market by 2030 as Agentic AI Redefines Data Center Architectures  As agentic AI puts CPUs back in the spotlight, Arm is sharpening its focus on the emerging opportunity. Here are the key takeaways from Mohamed Awad, Arm’s EVP and General Manager of the Cloud AI Business Unit, and Ravi Malhotra, Director of Solutions Product Management, as reported by TrendForce on-site at the OCP Global Summit 2026.  3 Specialized CPU Roles in AI Data Centers Awad elaborated on how the CPU is critical and highly optimized for specific roles in modern AI infrastructure, including AI Head Node, Cloud-Native CPUs, and Agentic CPUs.  “The head node is all about co-design. Its primary responsibility is to keep the accelerator from sitting idle...So the head node has been optimized to keep that accelerator productive as much of the time as possible. It’s responsible for scheduling, for moving data, for managing memory,” he said.  Then here comes Cloud Native CPUs. According to Awad, high core count custom CPUs enable VMs that perform and are efficient and scale. And custom built DPUs are designed to support that networking, that storage, that security, that control plane.  Lastly, Agentic AI is rapidly becoming the AI workload. “An agent is just a virtual user. A virtual user who never sleeps… It means the CPU is more important than ever. That’s why CPU demand is going through the roof.”  Against this backdrop, Arm, citing research projections, notes that the CPU market is expected to surge from $52B in 2026 to $300B by 2030.  Dual-Track Infrastructure: Pairing AI Racks with CPU Racks Malhotra highlighted that the infrastructure for agentic AI fundamentally consists of two complementary parts.  “On one side, you have got AI racks or AI infrastructure, which is focused on agentic reasoning and planning,” he explained. In this domain, the primary goal is running various types of models to deliver high token throughput—maximizing tokens per second, per watt, and per dollar.  “On the other hand, you’ve got CPU racks. All of the agentic tooling and orchestration is typically going to run on these CPU racks,” Malhotra noted.   AGI CPU in Focus To address the demand spurred by agentic AI, Malhotra highlighted the breakthrough of Arm’s AGI CPU, the first server-grade CPU silicon designed by the company.  “Now when we’re designing AGI CPU, we kept three things in mind: high performance, scalability, and efficiency, and we made some deliberate design choices. We took the latest third generation Neoverse core, where we worked on a lot of optimizations in partnerships with hyperscalers. We focus on reducing the memory latency, ensuring that there’s high memory bandwidth per core so that there’s no contention, and at the same time, we are ensuring that there’s linear scalability,” Malhotra emphasized. [OCP in Focus] SK hynix Drives up to 5x Faster TTFT with Memory-Centric AI Rack-Scale System; HBF Expands Capacity by 14x  To break free from the ongoing memory crunch, SK hynix is pushing the boundaries of AI infrastructure beyond HBM. At the OCP Global Summit 2026, SK hynix Senior Vice President Hoshik Kim introduced MARS (Memory-Centric AI Rack-Scale System), a disaggregated rack-scale architecture designed to seamlessly coordinate compute and memory resources.  Notably, Kim also spotlighted the progress of HBF (High Bandwidth Flash), targeting the industry's pressing capacity constraints. Here is TrendForce’s on-site summary of his key remarks.  MARS: Boosting TTFT up to 5x to Solve Processor-Centric Cluster Bottlenecks  According to Kim, traditional processor-centric architectures face severe structural limitations in distributed computing clusters. These include resource imbalance—where idle memory on one server cannot be easily shared with another—as well as rigid scalability, where adding memory requires purchasing an entire new server node. Consequently, operators are forced into GPU over-provisioning, driving up TCO and creating system inefficiencies.  “By memory disaggregation, this decouples memory from traditional CPU/GPU server constraints, creating a dedicated, massive memory pool... we can actually move from a per-server memory headroom to a pool-level efficiency," Kim said.  As explained by Kim, MARS is a disaggregated rack-scale memory system that coordinates compute and memory as a shared infrastructure. “Now we are expanding this concept of the memory tray-level memory pool as a rack-scale memory pool.”  Highlighting the real-world performance gains enabled by MARS, Kim noted: “We applied this one into a multi-turn AI agentic AI inferencing service. And then by providing this system, we can actually consume and store this exploding KV cache through this multi-turn AI agents into a shared memory system without exhausting GPU memory and storage systems.”  “So if you look at this graph, we have a very good 3 to 5 times improvement in TTFT (Time To First Token) over recomputation, which is quite impressive, especially when you talk about this tail latency, tail latency is dramatically reduced.”  HBF: Delivering 14x HBM Capacity with Sampling Set for 2028  SK hynix also elaborated on its progress with High Bandwidth Flash (HBF, referred to as HBMF during the presentation), highlighting its key performance strengths.  “Basically, HBM is a good memory... So HBF expands this HBM-class bandwidth to rack-scale capability/capacity... HBF is typically half the bandwidth of HBM, but more like 14 times higher capacity than HBM," Kim said.  He confirmed that product development is well on track. “Recently in July, we released OCP HBF spec version 0.7... expecting to release spec version 1.0 early next year, and currently developing HBF concept prototype, and we'll sample HBF Cube available early 2028.”  Details here: https://pse.is/9qspxr

CFO Colette Kress said during the earnings call that FY2028 revenue is expected to grow by around 70%, with the outlook constrained primarily by supply chain capacity rather than a lack of market demand.  Vera Rubin Platform Enters Full Production Commenting on current market developments, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang said AI has reached an inflection point, with the technology now capable of performing useful work and generating productive, economically valuable tokens. He emphasized that the global AI infrastructure buildout is advancing at full speed, while NVIDIA’s latest Vera Rubin platform has entered full-scale production. Huang added that companies will eventually operate multiple AI agents on a continuous basis, potentially driving a 15- to 100-fold increase in overall computing requirements.  Gross Margins Face Downward Pressure Despite maintaining a strong gross margin of 75% in the second quarter, NVIDIA is expected to face mounting cost pressures. Kress noted that surging AI demand has tightened memory supply, with extreme pricing conditions exceeding the company’s previous expectations and likely to persist through next year. NVIDIA has therefore lowered its gross margin outlook. The company expects gross margin to decline to 74% in the third quarter and bottom out at 71–72% in the fourth quarter before recovering to 72–73% in the first quarter of FY2028.  Huang Addresses Circular Financing Concerns NVIDIA’s substantial investments in frontier AI labs have raised market concerns over so-called “circular financing.” Kress acknowledged these concerns but said NVIDIA views these labs as once-in-a-century companies, with limited investment risk and attractive potential returns. AI labs requiring balance-sheet support are expected to account for approximately one-quarter of NVIDIA’s business next year. Huang added that NVIDIA provides a complete AI factory platform that is fundamentally different from custom inference chips designed for individual functions.
